entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marbodius of Rennes (c. 1035 – September 18, 1123) emerged as a pivotal intellectual figure in the late 11th and early 12th centuries, serving first as Archdeacon and schoolmaster at Angers, France, before his elevation to Bishop of Rennes in 1096. His career spanned a period of significant ecclesiastical reform and intellectual flourishing in Western Europe, positioning him as a respected poet, hagiographer, and hymnologist whose works contributed significantly to the didactic and moral literature of the Gregorian Reform era. His writings, particularly his moralizing poetry and detailed hagiographies, offer valuable insights into the spiritual and intellectual currents of high medieval France, reflecting the broader societal shifts towards clerical education and a more structured church hierarchy under figures like Pope Gregory VII.

His primary literary output includes the *Liber decem capitulorum*, a collection of moralizing poems on vices and virtues, and his most widely circulated work, *Liber lapidum seu de gemmis*, a lapidary describing the properties of sixty precious stones, blending scientific observation with allegorical and magical beliefs. As Bishop of Rennes from 1096 until his death, Marbodius actively participated in the spiritual and temporal governance of his diocese, working to reform monastic life and strengthen episcopal authority, often navigating complex relationships with local nobility and the Duke of Brittany. He also authored numerous hymns, saints' lives, and a biography of Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the Abbey of Fontevraud.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marbodius of Rennes significantly impacted medieval intellectual life through his widely disseminated poetic and hagiographic works, particularly the *Liber lapidum*, which became a standard reference for natural philosophy and symbolism for centuries. As a bishop, he also played a key role in the ecclesiastical and moral reforms within Brittany.
